body:
The documentation for the `data_array` property states this:
"Note: The returned array is copied and any changes to it will not update the original property value. See PackedByteArray for more details." (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_streampeerbuffer.html)
According to this note, this behaviour is expected. You can use the setter to change the `data_array` property.

I had read that before reporting this, but the documentation is a bit ambiguous about what it means by "the returned array" (does it mean a direct reference [it should not be returning anything; it's a direct reference], using get_data_array(), or both?), so I experimented with PackedByteArray.

PackedByteArray behaves in the expected manner, so a direct reference to data_array should behave identically. Returning a new PackedByteArray when directly accessing data_array would be a major design flaw. Frankly, returning a copy is a bad design decision as well under any circumstances. It should ALWAYS be a reference to the underlying PackedByteArray. Making a copy introduces an unnecessary performance hit that can range from minor to major.

> I had read that before reporting this, but the documentation is a bit ambiguous about what it means by "the returned array" (does it mean a direct reference [it should not be returning anything; it's a direct reference], using get_data_array(), or both?), so I experimented with PackedByteArray.
> 
> PackedByteArray behaves in the expected manner, so a direct reference to data_array should behave identically.

"Note: Packed arrays are always passed by reference. To get a copy of an array that can be modified independently of the original array, use [duplicate()](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_packedbytearray.html#class-packedbytearray-method-duplicate). This is not the case for built-in properties and methods. The returned packed array of these are a copies, and changing it will not affect the original value. To update a built-in property you need to modify the returned array, and then assign it to the property again." (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_packedbytearray.html#class-packedbytearray)

> Returning a new PackedByteArray when directly accessing data_array would be a major design flaw. Frankly, returning a copy is a bad design decision as well under any circumstances. It should ALWAYS be a reference to the underlying PackedByteArray. Making a copy introduces an unnecessary performance hit that can range from minor to major.

I'm not too familiar with Godot's codebase, but by taking a quick look:
The `data_array` on the C++ side of things is `Vector<uint8_t>`, but on the scripting side it's converted into a `PackedByteArray` when accessed, so it's not the original reference.

Hi there 👋 It appears there is some confusion in this thread, so I'd like to help clear it up.

> "Note: The returned array is copied and any changes to it will not update the original property value. See PackedByteArray for more details." (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_streampeerbuffer.html)

First off - yes, `get_data_array()` does indeed return a copy (it is returned by value, not by reference):

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/0793c626d2e203c6db04656853f8088478181888/core/io/stream_peer.h#L150

As @DinkeyKing noted, this means any changes to the returned value does not affect the underlying buffer in `StreamPeerBuffer`. This is by design.

> Frankly, returning a copy is a bad design decision as well under any circumstances. It should ALWAYS be a reference to the underlying PackedByteArray. Making a copy introduces an unnecessary performance hit that can range from minor to major.

There is no major design flaw happening here :)
What you're saying would normally be correct, but one fact you're missing is that `Vector` is a [copy-on-write](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copy-on-write) data structure. That means that it _doesn't actually_ copy the buffer when returning it to you. Instead, it returns you the original array, without wasting time by copying it, but it hands it to you without ownership. Only when you (or someone else) attempts to _modify_ the array for the first time, the costly copy is _actually_ performed. 

> Note: Packed arrays are always passed by reference. To get a copy of an array that can be modified independently of the original array, use [duplicate()](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_packedbytearray.html#class-packedbytearray-method-duplicate).

This is a different thing altogether again. `Variant` uses _shared reference semantics_ on top of `PackedByteArray` (and other packed types). When the engine returns something to you, it is returned as a copy-on-write copy. However, when you pass it around yourself within GDScript, it is handled as a reference instead.
Since this is an engine function, the returned value is a copy-on-write copy, and not passed by reference.

> The data_array on the C++ side of things is Vector<uint8_t>, but on the scripting side it's converted into a PackedByteArray when accessed, so it's not the original reference.

`PackedByteArray` is actually just an alias of `Vector<uint8_t>` :)

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/0793c626d2e203c6db04656853f8088478181888/core/variant/variant.h#L76

> There is no major design flaw happening here :)

I disagree. Returning a copy of the ```PackedByteArray``` upon usage of ```StreamPeerBuffer.data_array``` is a design flaw. Doubly so since a ```StreamPeerBuffer.data_array``` access changes the normal behavior of ```PackedByteArray```. A class's behavior should never change just because its entry point changes. A class should be relied upon to always behave the same.

> A class's behavior should never change just because its entry point changes. A class should be relied upon to always behave the same.

The class behaves the same all within `Core`, it's `Variant` that treats it differently specifically.
It's definitely a gotcha with the engine's design, but usually it's not noticed because it's generally you don't modify arrays owned by other data structures.
As to that point, it is still unclear to me why you want to modify `StreamPeerBuffer's` array in the first place. Would you mind explaining what you expect to happen?
If you just want to modify the data, and use it elsewhere, it would be easy to just duplicate the data and modify your own version:
```gdscript
var my_data := stream_peer_buffer.get_data_array()
my_data.append_array(other_array)
my_function(my_data)
```

> As to that point, it is still unclear to me why you want to modify StreamPeerBuffer's array in the first place.

I have incoming network data from ```StreamPeerTCP```. ```StreamPeerBuffer``` is where the incoming network data are placed for parsing.

Say that data are received from ```StreamPeerTCP```. The packet data indicate that the complete packet requires 500 bytes, but the program receives 300 bytes on StreamPeerTCP. The 300 bytes are then appended to ```StreamPeerBuffer.data_array```, and then the ```StreamPeerBuffer``` is passed to the parser. The parser finds that there is not enough data, so it resets the read pointer to the start of the packet, stops parsing, and the program waits for the next receive event to occur. The 300 bytes stay in ```StreamPeerBuffer``` while the program waits for the next receive event.

On then next receive event, 400 bytes are received. They are appended to ```StreamPeerBuffer```, and the buffer is passed to the parser.  The parser finds enough bytes to complete the packet, so it goes about parsing. The packet needs 500 bytes, but the buffer has 700 bytes. The ```StreamPeerBuffer``` pointer remains at 700 while waiting to receive more data. The partial packet information remaining indicates that the packet needs 10 more bytes, so the parser stops and waits.

On the next receive event, 10 bytes are received. They are appended to ```StreamPeerBuffer```, and the buffer is passed to the parser.  The parse finds enough bytes to complete the packet, so it goes about parsing. When finished parsing, all data have been received, so the ```StreamPeerBuffer``` is cleared of data and is ready to receive more.

Without the ability to append to ```StreamPeerBuffer.data_array```, this process breaks. It is otherwise an ideal object to use for this purpose, as it has all the necessary supporting functions. I could create another GDScript class that duplicates this functionality, and I will have to until ```StreamPeerBuffer``` provides support for this, but it will be slower (GDScript vs C++) and an unnecessary duplication of something that is 99.9% there already.

```StreamPeerBuffer``` could provide a new method (something like ```get_data_unmodified()```) that returns a reference to the underlying ```data_array``` instead of a copy, and that would solve the problem.

Thank you for the explanation, I think I may understand your use-case now :)
Here's my advice - though take it with a grain of salt, since I'm not well versed in Godot's packet management.

Normally, I'd expect the full data to be transmitted in a single event. This is what the `StreamPeerBuffer` interface was designed for, after all - without you having to concatenate packets manually.

If you still need to concatenate packets yourself, this should be trivial with a local `PackedByteArray` which you intermittently append to:

```gdscript
var current_data: PackedByteArray

current_data.append_array(stream_peer_buffer.get_data_array())

if parser.parse(current_data):
    current_data.clear()
```

This has the benefit of your `StreamPeer` being able to accept other data in the meantime, in case this is your use-case for not pushing the full data in a single event.

You could also manually [put more data](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_streampeer.html#class-streampeer-method-put-partial-data) into the `StreamPeer` that holds your `StreamPeerBuffer`. I'm not sure this can be done safely, but it's worth a try? This calls `StreamPeerBuffer::put_data`, which would be the expected way of appending data to it. This function is not exposed to GDScript because it operates on pointers.

I hope this helps. If it doesn't, I'm afraid I'll have to hand off to folks that know their way around networking!

TCP makes no guarantees that packets will remain intact. It explicitly guarantees that packets may be broken up in varying ways, and reassembled in varying ways. All it really guarantees is that the packets will eventually arrive, and in the order in which they were sent. In theory, a 1000-byte packet could be received as a thousand packets consisting of one byte each.

This is not a flaw, but an implementation limitation related to the complexity of cross-language interoperability. The problem is that you can't actually access a property of a built-in type or native class. Each property is exposed as a setter and getter that are called when you interact with the property.

The internal structure is not necessarily the same type as the exposed property, the value can be dynamically calculated in the getter (when you read the property) and processed in the setter (when you assign a new value to the property). For example, you can run into the same thing in GDScript if you implement a property like this:

```gdscript
var my_property: Array:
    set(value):
        # Here you can also validate the value.
        _my_property.assign(value)
    get:
        return _my_property.duplicate()

# Imagine that the internal property has a different type.
var _my_property: Array
```

Yes, it's quite non-obvious. But if this is a design flaw, it's an API flaw. If the property had only setter and getter methods, this behavior would be less unexpected. But it would be less convenient and we still can't change it until 5.0 due to compatibility.

In theory, we could detect a call to a non-`const` (i.e. most likely mutable) method on a built-in property and produce a warning using the GDScript static analyzer. But this does not guarantee the absence of false negatives due to the dynamic nature of GDScript.

I'll try working around it with a custom class that reimplements  the relevant parts of StreamPeerBuffer. Just passing a PackedByteArray to the parser almost works, but the parser needs to be able to know and set the buffer pointer, which PackedByteArray can't do. By the time I add the necessary support code to the parser, I will have reimplemented most of StreamPeerBuffer anyway.

I created a custom class that implements the parts of StreamPeerBuffer that I use, so now I can use data_array.append() as I had originally planned. Being able to append to the array fixes the problems I was having.
